description: At the end of these words, do not pronounce a separate m or b. The preceding vowel is nasalized: let some air pass through your nose as you say it.

thoughts: Final pt varies by word: sept sounds the t, concept sounds both letters, and exempt sounds neither.
description: At the end of a French word, pt has no single fixed pronunciation. In sept, the p is silent and the t sounds like English t. In concept, both letters sound, as in English “kept.” In exempt, both are silent.

thoughts: At the end of common French words, ps is usually silent. The word laps is an exception: both letters are pronounced.
description: Usually, do not pronounce either letter in final ps: temps sounds like “tahn” with a nasal vowel. In laps, say both sounds, /ps/, as at the end of English “lapse.”

example_words.cultural_context: A common word for time and weather
Seen in English expressions such as “corps de ballet”
Used in the phrase “un laps de temps,” meaning a span of time
